{{short description|Concept in axiomatic set theory}}
{{Use shortened footnotes|date=May 2021}}  
In [[axiomatic set theory]], the '''axiom of union''' is one of the [[axiom]]s of [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]]. This axiom was introduced by [[Ernst Zermelo]].{{r|Zermelo1908}}

Informally, the axiom states that if {{tmath|X}} is a [[set (mathematics)|set]] of sets, then the [[Union (set theory)#Arbitrary union|union]] of all sets in {{tmath|X}} is still a set. In more basic terms, for each set {{tmath|X}} there is a set {{tmath|Y}} whose elements are precisely the elements of the elements of {{tmath|X}}.

== Formal statement ==
In the [[formal language]] of the Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms, the axiom reads:<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jech |first=Thomas J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wmOISAAACAAJ |title=Set Theory |date=1997 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-63048-7 |edition=2nd |pages=6 |language=en}}</ref>
<math display="block">\forall X\, \exists Y\, \forall u\, (u \in Y \leftrightarrow \exists z\, (u \in z \land z \in X))</math>
or in words:
:[[Given any]] [[Set (mathematics)|set]] ''X'', [[Existential quantification|there is]] a set ''Y'' such that, for any element ''u'', ''u'' [[Element (set theory)|is a member of]] ''Y'' [[if and only if]] there is a set ''z'' such that ''u'' is a member of ''z'' [[logical conjunction|and]] ''z'' is a member of ''X''.
or, more simply:
:For any set <math>X</math>, there is a set <math>\bigcup X</math> which consists of just the elements of the elements of that set <math>X</math>.

== Consequences ==
The axiom of union allows one to unpack a set of sets and thus create a flatter set. 
Together with the [[axiom of pairing]], it implies that for any two sets {{tmath|A}} and {{tmath|B}}, their [[Union (set theory)#Union of two sets|binary union]] {{tmath|A \cup B}} is also a set.

Together with the [[axiom schema of replacement]], the axiom of union implies that one can form the union of a [[Indexed family|family]] of sets indexed by a set.

The axiom of union is often used to construct the [[Set-theoretic limit|limit]] of an infinite sequence of sets {{tmath|X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq X_2 \subseteq \cdots}}. For example, it can be used to construct the [[supremum]] of any set of [[ordinal number]]s.<ref name="Oman10" />

== Weaker form ==
In the context of set theories which include the [[axiom schema of separation]], the axiom of union is sometimes stated in a weaker form which only produces a [[superset]] of the union of a set. For example, Kunen{{r|Kunen1980}} states the axiom as 
<math display="block">\forall \mathcal{F} \,\exists A \, \forall Y\, \forall x [(x \in Y \land Y \in \mathcal{F}) \Rightarrow x \in A]</math>
to facilitate its verification in various [[model (mathematical logic)|model]]s. This form is logically equivalent to
<math display="block">\forall \mathcal{F} \,\exists A \forall x [ [\exists Y (x \in Y \land Y \in \mathcal{F}) ] \Rightarrow x \in A].</math>
Compared to the axiom stated at the top of this section, this variation asserts only one direction of the implication, rather than both directions.

== Independence ==
In its full generality, the axiom of union is [[Independence (mathematical logic)|independent]] from the rest of the ZFC-axioms. It is the only axiom that asserts the existence of [[Singular cardinal|singular]] [[strong limit cardinal]]s such as {{tmath|\beth_\omega}} ([[Beth number|beth-omega]], the limit of the sequence {{tmath|\aleph_0, 2^{\aleph_0}, 2^{2^{\aleph_0} }, \ldots}}). Concretely, if {{tmath|\kappa}} is a singular strong limit cardinal, then the set of sets {{tmath|X}} such that {{tmath|\vert X \vert < \kappa}} and {{tmath|\vert y \vert < \kappa}} for all {{tmath|y}} in the [[transitive closure]] of {{tmath|X}}{{efn|This condition is known as {{tmath|X}} being ''pseudo-hereditarily of cardinality less than {{tmath|\kappa}}'', to distinguish it from the stronger condition of being ''hereditarily of cardinality less than {{tmath|\kappa}}'', which requires the transitive closure itself to have cardinality less than {{tmath|\kappa}}.}} forms a [[model (mathematical logic)|model]] of {{tmath|\text{ZFC} - \text{Union} }} (the ZFC axioms minus the axiom of union).<ref name="Oman10" />

However, many results in ZF(C) remain valid even without the axiom of union. The [[axiom schema of replacement]] allows one to form a union if one can construct a set of the same or larger [[cardinality]], together with a definable surjection from it onto that union, which can often be achieved with the [[axiom of power set]]. For example, the binary union {{tmath|A \cup B}} can be constructed when the cardinalities {{tmath|\vert A \vert}} and {{tmath|\vert B \vert}} are [[Comparability|comparable]], since without loss of generality one can assume that {{tmath|\vert A \vert \le \vert B \vert}} and {{tmath|2 \le \vert B \vert}}, and then
<math display="block>|A \cup B| \le |A| + |B| \le 2 \cdot |B| \le |B| \cdot |B| = |B \times B| \le |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(B))|</math>
where the final inequality follows from the [[Cartesian product#Set-theoretic definition|definition of the Cartesian product]] using the [[Kuratowski ordered pair]].

Assuming the [[axiom of choice]], the [[well-ordering theorem]] can be proved without the axiom of union, which can be used to show that {{tmath|\bigcup X}} exists ''as long as the cardinalities of all sets in {{tmath|X}} are bounded''. This condition is always true for finite unions, or more generally when {{tmath|X}} only contains sets with a finite number of infinite cardinalities. Conversely, assuming the consistency of ZF, there exists a model of {{tmath|\text{ZFC} - \text{Union} }} such that {{tmath|\bigcup X}} ''never'' exists when {{tmath|X}} contains sets with an infinite number of infinite cardinalities.<ref name="Oman10">{{cite journal | last=Oman | first=Greg | title=On the axiom of union | journal=Archive for Mathematical Logic | volume=49 | issue=3 | date=2010 | issn=0933-5846 | doi=10.1007/s00153-009-0163-1 | pages=283–289 | url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s00153-009-0163-1 | access-date=2026-01-31| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Relation to Intersection ==
There is no corresponding axiom of [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]]. If <math>A</math> is a ''nonempty'' set containing <math>E</math>, it is possible to form the intersection <math>\bigcap A</math> using the [[axiom schema of specification]] as
<math display="block">\bigcap A = \{c\in E:\forall D(D\in A\Rightarrow c\in D)\},</math>
so no separate axiom of intersection is necessary. (If ''A'' is the [[empty set]], then trying to form the intersection of ''A'' as
:{''c'': for all ''D'' in ''A'', ''c'' is in ''D''}
is not permitted by the axioms. Moreover, if such a set existed, then it would contain every set in the "universe", but the notion of a [[universal set]] is antithetical to Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory.)
